paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Counter-Reformation, which also goes by the names Catholic Revival and Catholic Reformation, was a time of renewed strength for the Catholic Church. It began partly as a reply to the Protestant Reformation, partly as a different path from it, and partly out of some of the same concerns. It grew out of the decisions of the Council of Trent. As a period, it is often dated from that council, which met from 1545 to 1563, to the end of Europe's wars of religion in 1648, though those dates are disputed.

paragraphs.heading: Old problems
paragraphs.text: Many of the church's troubles had been known for a long time. Popes favouring their relatives, rich bishops who stayed away from their dioceses, and bishops busy with worldly power were seen as lasting scandals. In the fifty years before the Reformation, bishops shut down decadent monasteries and convents more often, and programmes to educate parish priests also grew more common. Religious orders had first tried to reform themselves back in the 14th century.

paragraphs.heading: The Council of Trent
paragraphs.text: Pope Paul III, who reigned from 1534 to 1549, is seen as the first pope of the Counter-Reformation. He opened the Council of Trent and gave it the job of reforming the church's institutions. It took on corrupt bishops and priests, the selling of indulgences and other money abuses. At the same time, the council kept the basic shape of the medieval church: its sacraments, its religious orders and its doctrine.

paragraphs.heading: What it produced
paragraphs.text: The movement turned out works defending and arguing for Catholic belief, drives against corruption, inner reform, spiritual movements, new religious orders and new styles of art and music. Seminaries were set up to train priests properly in the spiritual life and in the church's theology. New movements stressed devotion and a personal bond with Christ, among them the Spanish mystics and the French school of spirituality. There was a political side too, including regional Inquisitions, and war and unfair laws forced many religious refugees to move.

paragraphs.heading: New kinds of priests
paragraphs.text: To meet new needs in spreading the faith, groups of regular clergy formed: priests who took special vows but did not have to share in a monastery's round of prayer. They taught, preached and heard confession under a bishop's direct authority, without being tied to one parish. In Italy the first such group was the Theatines, founded in 1524, and others followed, including the Jesuits, recognised in 1540. The Capuchins, born from a 1526 call to return the Franciscan rule to its first purity, became known for public preaching. Philip Neri's Oratorians drew people in with music and singing.

paragraphs.heading: Mission and winning back
paragraphs.text: One main aim was mission to parts of the world that mostly Catholic nations had colonized. Another was to win back countries such as Sweden and England. Both had been Catholic since Europe first became Christian but had been lost to the Reformation.

paragraphs.heading: A disputed name
paragraphs.text: The name translates the German word Gegenreformation. German historians coined it in the late 1700s as a negative label for Catholic repression, and writers such as Leopold von Ranke spread it in the 1800s. Catholic historians avoided it. In 1880 the Protestant historian Wilhelm Maurenbrecher brought in the term Catholic Reformation. The historian Massimo Firpo separates the two ideas: a Catholic Reformation about caring for souls and renewing the clergy, and a Counter-Reformation about defending orthodoxy, repressing dissent and reasserting church authority.
